Here's a surprising place to start: an LLM never actually sees your words.

Before anything else happens, your prompt is chopped into pieces called **tokens**, and each token is swapped for a number. The model only ever works with those numbers.

[KEY]An LLM reads tokens (chunks of text turned into numbers), not words or letters.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine typing "unbelievable". A tokenizer might split it into "un", "believ", and "able", then turn each chunk into an ID like 403, 8821, 912 (these numbers are made up for illustration; every model has its own). GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens to choose from.[/EX]

[Q]
Why does a model work with tokens instead of whole words?
A) Every English word is already stored as one token
B) Chunks can be reused to build any word, even rare ones
C) Tokens let the model look up the answer in a database
D) Tokens are always exactly one letter long
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Chunks can be reused to build any word, even rare ones
replies.raw:
Right: a fixed set of reusable chunks can build any word, including ones the model has never seen whole.

Now for what the model does with those numbers. Each token becomes a long list of numbers called an **embedding**, and similar meanings end up with similar lists. But a token's meaning depends on its neighbors, so the model uses **attention** to let the other words in the sentence adjust each token.

[KEY]Attention lets surrounding words reshape what each token means in context.[/KEY]

[EX]Take "bank" in two sentences. In "I sat on the bank of the river", attention to "river" pushes "bank" toward the shore meaning. In "I put cash in the bank", attention to "cash" pushes it toward money. The token for "bank" starts out identical in both, and context does the sorting.[/EX]

[Q]
In "I sat on the bank of the river", what tells the model which "bank" is meant?
A) The first word of the sentence
B) The model always picks the money meaning
C) A dictionary entry that picks one meaning
D) Attention to the nearby word "river"
ANS: D
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) The first word of the sentence
replies.raw:
Not quite. The first word, "I", is the same in both bank sentences, so it can't be what separates the two meanings.

Look at what actually differs: "river" in one sentence, "cash" in the other. Attention lets the token for "bank" take in information from those neighboring words, and that shifts its meaning toward shore or money.

[EX]Try a new one: "The bat flew out of the cave." Which words should "bat" pay attention to? "flew" and "cave" pull it toward the animal. In "He swung the bat and hit a homer", words like "swung" and "homer" pull it toward baseball. The word "bat" is identical both times, but the words around it differ.[/EX]

[Q]
In "He swung the bat and hit a homer", which words most help the model pick the baseball meaning of "bat"?
A) "He" at the start of the sentence
B) None, since the model just guesses
C) "swung" and "homer"
D) "the" and "and"
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) "swung" and "homer"
replies.raw:
Yes, "swung" and "homer" are the words that tip "bat" toward baseball, and now you can see why the first word couldn't do that job.

Let's keep going. So far we've turned text into numbers and let context shape each token's meaning. The last step is the one the whole system exists for: **next-token prediction**.

The model reads everything so far and produces a probability for every token in its vocabulary, then one token gets picked and added to the text. Then the whole process repeats for the next one.

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly predicting a probability for each possible next token, picking one, and repeating.[/KEY]

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". "mat" or "floor" or "couch" would each get a decent share of the probability, but "volcano" gets almost none. Now take "The capital of France is ___". One token, "Paris", gets nearly all the probability, so the model is very confident there.[/EX]

Notice what's missing: no lookup in a database of answers. The model is scoring likely continuations, which is also why it can sound sure of itself without being right.

[Q]
When a model writes "Paris" after "The capital of France is", what has it done?
A) Predicted the most likely next token
B) Checked a map of European cities
C) Copied a sentence from its training data word for word
D) Searched a database for a stored fact
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Predicted the most likely next token
replies.raw:
Correct. "Paris" wins because it takes nearly all the probability, and no map or database is involved.
